guide.summary: Unit 1 develops the language of change for functions: average rates of change, increasing/decreasing and concavity, polynomial zeros and end behavior, rational functions with asymptotes and holes, transformations, equivalent forms (division, binomial theorem), and choosing and validating function models.

sections.heading: Rates of change
sections.body: Average rate of change of f on [a, b] = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a), the slope of the secant line. A function is increasing on an interval if output increases as input increases. Concave up: rates of change are increasing (graph bends upward); concave down: rates of change are decreasing. Points of inflection occur where concavity changes. For data in a table with equal input spacing, constant first differences indicate linear, constant second differences indicate quadratic, and constant nth differences indicate degree n.

sections.heading: Polynomial functions
sections.body: A polynomial of degree n has at most n real zeros and at most n − 1 extrema. A zero of odd multiplicity crosses the x-axis; even multiplicity touches and turns. End behavior is governed by the leading term: even degree with positive leading coefficient → both ends up; odd degree with positive leading coefficient → down on the left, up on the right. Complex zeros of polynomials with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs. Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x) (symmetric about the y-axis); odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x) (symmetric about the origin). Polynomial inequalities are solved with a sign chart.

sections.heading: Rational functions
sections.body: Factor numerator and denominator. A common factor cancels and leaves a hole. A remaining zero of the denominator is a vertical asymptote. End behavior: if degree of numerator < degree of denominator, horizontal asymptote y = 0; if equal, y = ratio of leading coefficients; if numerator degree is one greater, a slant asymptote found by polynomial division. Zeros of a rational function are zeros of the numerator not canceled by the denominator.

sections.heading: Transformations, equivalent forms, and models
sections.body: g(x) = af(b(x − h)) + k: vertical dilation by a (reflect if a < 0), horizontal dilation by 1/b, shift right h and up k. Equivalent forms reveal different features: factored form shows zeros, standard form shows end behavior; polynomial long division rewrites rational expressions; the binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ using combinations. Choose a model by examining rates of change and context (linear: constant rate; quadratic: linearly changing rate; cubic or higher for more complex behavior), and consider domain restrictions and assumptions.

keyTakeaways: Average rate of change = secant slope.
Concave up ↔ increasing rate of change.
Common factor → hole; leftover denominator zero → VA.
Degree comparison gives horizontal or slant asymptotes.
Constant nth differences → degree n polynomial.
commonMistakes: Calling a canceled factor a vertical asymptote.
Forgetting the negative sign when transforming horizontally (shift right for x − h).
Confusing increasing function with concave up.
Using the wrong leading term for end behavior after expanding.
Forgetting to exclude points where the denominator is zero in inequalities.
examTips: Justify concavity with 'the average rates of change over consecutive equal intervals are increasing.'
Write end behavior using limits: lim_(x→∞) f(x) = ∞.
In rational-function questions, factor first and check for holes before asymptotes.
Sign charts: test each interval and include/exclude endpoints carefully.
guide.cramSheet:
**ARC:** [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a)

**Concavity:** up = rates increasing · down = rates decreasing

**Polynomials:** degree n → ≤ n zeros, ≤ n − 1 extrema · odd mult crosses, even touches · leading term → end behavior

**Rational:** cancel → hole · leftover denom zero → VA · deg N < D → y = 0 · equal → ratio · N = D + 1 → slant

**Transform:** af(b(x − h)) + k

**Differences:** constant nth → degree n

practice.prompt: The function h is defined by h(x) = (x² − 9)/(x² − 2x − 3).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the x-coordinate of any hole in the graph of h, and find the y-value that the hole corresponds to. Show the work that leads to your answer.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Write an equation for each vertical asymptote and each horizontal asymptote of h. Justify using the factored form.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Find all real zeros of h.

rubric.description: For x slightly greater than −1: numerator (x + 3) ≈ 2 > 0, denominator (x + 1) → 0⁺, so h → +∞.
x = −3 (x = 3 is excluded as a hole).

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Factoring: h(x) = (x − 3)(x + 3)/[(x − 3)(x + 1)]. The common factor (x − 3) creates a hole at x = 3. For x ≠ 3, h(x) = (x + 3)/(x + 1), so the hole corresponds to y = 6/4 = 3/2.

B. After canceling, the denominator x + 1 is zero at x = −1, so x = −1 is a vertical asymptote. The numerator and denominator have the same degree (2) with leading coefficients 1 and 1, so y = 1 is the horizontal asymptote.

C. As x → −1 from the right, x + 3 → 2 (positive) and x + 1 → 0 through positive values, so h(x) = (x + 3)/(x + 1) → +∞.

D. The numerator of the simplified function is zero at x = −3. (x = 3 is not a zero because h is undefined there.) The only real zero is x = −3.
